items.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022
items.q: I heard you and Murray Horwitz on the air, a re-play of one of the albums you picked for that marvelous jazz review

ctx.x: I used to have one and it had to involve the diminution of the ego and of the — having more poetry of equality where everything stood at the same level. I got used to me having that it’s nice, but the fact is I just do it because I’ve always done it. And I try to punctuate with measure. I very seldom — I punctuate when I can’t get out of it. Question marks for example, I can’t find a way around, but usually I try to punctuate at the end of the line on the page would be where the period would be. And I sometimes…

I see. Well thank you for sharing that with me. I wanted to go back to this, I heard you and Murray Horwitz on the air, a re-play of one of the albums you picked for that marvelous jazz review and it was Cannonball and “Something Else.” And on the “Autumn Leaves” you called his solo “perfect, not a wrong note.” And I’m a huge Cannonball fan so it really caught my attention. And it’s been a while but can you recall why you felt it was perfect?

Why I felt it was perfect. Well Cannonball had a gift for connecting his notes in such a way that every one seemed like the right note. Now some other people like, again, Coletrane again would be more like challenging with the way his notes related to each other. He would create all these tensions within his music and even use things like quarter tones to challenge your ear a bit more. So the sense of rightness that this is the correct note doesn’t come into it in the same way that it would with Cannonball. With…
